title: Patience and Faith
english: From Cyril: That is, the wrath has all but slaughtered them, and laid them low like rams and bulls, sturdy and fat. To such people we might fairly say, “Come now, you rich, weep and wail over the miseries that are coming upon you” (James 5:1). And we will add to this the words, “You have lived in luxury and self-indulgence on the earth; you have fattened your hearts as on a day of slaughter” (James 5:5). For such were the leaders of the Jews. They grazed, in a manner of speaking, on a rich and spacious pasture: the gifts brought by the people. But once fattened, the wretches fell, as it were, on the sword of the Lord.
“Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord” (James 5:7).

From Cyril: For even if God puts off the punishment of sinners, he says, as he waits for their repentance, he does not do this because he has changed his mind, or because he is fond of those who sin, but to give them time to turn back. Having spoken of the punishment of the unjust, he fittingly urges those who have been wronged to be patient as they await the coming of the Lord. At the same time he forbids them to have anything to do with oaths, and tells them to give their time to prayer and psalm-singing, to have faith toward the priests of God and love toward one another, so as to pray for one another. Elijah is brought forward as the proof of the strength of prayer. And last comes how great the reward is when sinners turn back.
“But above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or with any other oath” (James 5:12).

From Cyril: Let the witness of our life be surer than an oath. But if someone shameless, not abashed by your life, dares to put you on oath, let your “Yes, yes” and “No, no” stand in place of the oath (Matthew 5:37). This is why he forbids us to swear by heaven and earth: so that we do not give the creation a dignity that is above creation by making gods of these things. For those who swear, it says, swear by the greater, as the Apostle says (Hebrews 6:16).
On the First Letter of Saint Peter.
“In him, though you do not see him now, you believe and rejoice with a joy that cannot be told and is full of glory, as you obtain the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls” (1 Peter 1:8–9).
From Cyril: Unbelief, then, is a dreadful and grievous thing, but faith is the greatest of goods, since it is what brings about all salvation.

“For this reason it stands in Scripture: ‘See, I lay in Zion a cornerstone, chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will never be put to shame.’ To you, then, who believe, belongs the honor” (1 Peter 2:6–7).

From Cyril: He calls our Lord Jesus Christ a chosen stone, costly and precious, because he stands out in the glory and pre-eminence of the Godhead. And he calls him a cornerstone because through one faith he binds the two peoples, the one from Israel and the one from the nations, tightly together into a spiritual unity. But “whoever believes in him,” he says, “will never be put to shame.” And see how he grants to the afflicted their…

added_allusions.reason: Cyril's summary of the rest of the chapter (prayer and psalms, the elders, praying for one another, Elijah, turning a sinner back); summary, not quotation.

title: The Power of the Tongue
english: …freedom. He says, “I lay the chosen stone in the foundations of Zion” (Isaiah 28:16). And what good comes of it? “Whoever believes in him will never be put to shame.”
“Let him keep his tongue from evil” (1 Peter 3:10).

From Cyril: The lesson is worthy of the saints and brings salvation, and I say the instruction deserves every attention. For it is written, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who master it will eat its fruits” (Proverbs 18:21). And the disciple of Christ also said somewhere, “If anyone does not stumble in word, he is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body as well” (James 3:2). Great, then, is mastery of the tongue, just as, of course, not having it is a most grievous disease.

“In which he also went and preached to the spirits in prison, who had once disobeyed, when God’s patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built, in which a few, that is, eight souls, were brought safely through water” (1 Peter 3:19–20).

From Cyril: Here he answers the objection that some raise when they say, “If the incarnation is beneficial, why did he not become man many ages earlier?” For see: he went and preached even to the spirits in prison, to set free all of them who would have believed if he had taken flesh at that time and come among those on the earth. For these surely recognized him when he appeared even in the regions under the earth, and they enjoyed his appearing.

Going in his soul, he preached to those in Hades, seen as a soul among souls. When the gatekeepers of Hades saw him, they cowered (Job 38:17); gates of bronze were shattered and bars of iron were crushed (Psalm 107:16). And the Only-begotten called with authority to the souls who shared his condition, in keeping with the plan of salvation, saying to those in bonds, “Come out,” and to those in darkness, “Be uncovered” (Isaiah 49:9).

That is, he also preached to those in Hades, to set free all of them who would have believed if he had taken flesh and come to live among them in the time of their life; for these surely recognized him, even in Hades. For most of the plan carried out for us is beyond nature and beyond tradition. So, just as Christ, by his presence in the flesh, called out to all on earth on equal terms, and those who believed were helped, so too by his descent into Hades he set free from the bonds of death those who believed and recognized him. For the souls of those who had lived in idolatry and lawless debauchery, blinded, as it were, by their attachment to the flesh, had no strength to look toward the rays of the divine appearing, so as to recognize in faith the one who, to set all free (as far as it rested with him), appeared to those under the earth, preached to all alike, and showed justice together with his love for humankind. So those who fell away from such a kindness would have themselves to blame, for they had abandoned the…

added_allusions.reason: Gates of bronze and bars of iron broken also stand here; the verbs match Psalm 107:16 (LXX 106:16), which is printed.

title: Faith and Hospitality
english: …Creator and God of all, served man-hating demons, and lived as pleased them.
“Since, then, Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same mind,” and so on (1 Peter 4:1).

From Cyril: We must therefore understand that the Word of God, having become as we are, suffered in the flesh of his own free will. For this is how we have been baptized into his death (Romans 6:3): as into the death of one Son, who cannot suffer in the nature of the Godhead but can suffer in the flesh.

From Cyril: Because Christ is God, the disciple wisely and thoughtfully says that he suffered in the flesh, so withdrawing from suffering the ineffable nature, to which suffering is foreign. So the Word from God suffered in his own flesh, although his way is to have no part in suffering. Christ, then, is God: as God he cannot suffer, but in the flesh he can.
“If anyone serves, let it be as from the strength that God supplies” (1 Peter 4:11).

From Cyril: Let those who open their homes wide go out to meet their guests cheerful and eager, not as though they were giving anything, but rather as people who will themselves receive, and in two ways: first, they will enjoy the company of the guests they host, and then, on top of that, they will gain the reward of hospitality. When they welcome the brothers into their homes, let them not be distracted with much serving (Luke 10:40) or look for things beyond their means and their need. For excess is a burden everywhere and in everything. In those who want to show hospitality it breeds reluctance, and for those being entertained it turns into weariness.
Do not think it strange that hardships and afflictions and bodily illnesses come upon you (1 Peter 4:12); rather, in what seems hard, show that you are proved true.
On the Second Letter of Saint Peter.

“For we did not follow cleverly made-up myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For he received honor and glory from God the Father, when such a voice was borne to him by the majestic glory” (2 Peter 1:16–17).

From Cyril: For the arguments of the heretics are truly myths and human sophistries. Paul, wanting us to turn away from such people, writes: “Reject a heretical man after a first and second warning,” and so on (Titus 3:10). He is now beginning his attack on the heretics, since they, not having the truth, are forced to dress up the lie with elaborate words. But we are not like that, he says: we saw the truth with our own eyes, when we were with him on the mountain. We also have the prophets, who foretold this very truth to us, and so through what we saw the word of the prophets became surer for us (2 Peter 1:19); for what they said, Christ confirmed by his presence. And we are witnesses, who also heard the testimony…
translator_notes: The Greek text may be fragmented, and some sentences may be cut off at the edges.
The translation aims to preserve the original word order and meaning, while also conveying the author's voice and claims in natural literary prose.
The translation of σεσοφισμένοις μύθοις as 'clever myths' is preferred over 'sophisticated myths' to maintain the original meaning.
The verb γενηθέντες is in the aorist tense, indicating a completed action, and is translated as 'having become eyewitnesses'.
